title: Ulysses: occasion and date
short: A dramatic monologue written in October 1833, just after Arthur Hallam's death, and published in Poems (1842).
body: Tennyson drafted the poem within weeks of hearing (October 1833) that his closest friend Arthur Henry Hallam had died in Vienna. He later said it 'gave my feeling about the need of going forward, and braving the struggle of life' more simply than In Memoriam (Memoir I, 196). It was first printed in Poems (1842). The speaker is Ulysses (the Latin name of Homer's Odysseus), old and home again on Ithaca, but the poem's main source is not the Odyssey; it is Dante's Inferno XXVI, where Ulysses tells how he left home again to sail beyond the known world. Homer's own prophecy of a last journey (Odyssey XI, Tiresias) lies behind both. The poem is one of the founding examples of the Victorian dramatic monologue: a single voice, an implied audience, and a character revealed partly against his own intentions.

title: Ithaca
short: Ithaca, Ulysses' small rocky island kingdom off western Greece.
body: The 'still hearth' and 'barren crags' are Ithaca, the island Ulysses rules. Homer's Odysseus calls it rugged, 'but a good nurse of young men', and longs for it through twenty years of war and wandering (Odyssey IX.27-28). Tennyson reverses that longing: the homecoming that is the climax of Homer's epic becomes the starting point of restlessness. 'Still' carries both 'quiet' and 'motionless', and 'idle' both 'unoccupied' and 'futile', so the opening line already frames domestic kingship as a kind of paralysis. Critics who read Ulysses as heroic stress this sense of confinement; those who read him ironically (e.g. Chiasson) note how contemptuous his account of home and people is.

title: Penelope
short: Penelope, Ulysses' wife, who waited twenty years for him; here dismissed in two words.
body: In the Odyssey, the reunion with Penelope is the emotional climax of the poem (Odyssey XXIII). Tennyson's Ulysses mentions her only as 'an aged wife' he is 'match'd' with, a phrase that has drawn much comment. The coldness comes from Dante: his Ulysses says that neither tenderness for his son, nor duty to his old father, nor the love owed to Penelope could overcome his ardour to gain experience of the world (Inferno XXVI.94-99). Readers who see the poem as a straightforward expression of courage tend to pass over the line; readers like E. J. Chiasson take it as evidence that Tennyson shows a man who neglects duty and the 'softer affections'.

title: mete and dole
short: To measure out and hand out in portions: Ulysses describes kingship as grudging, mechanical distribution.
body: 'Mete' (Old English metan, to measure) and 'dole' (from Old English dal, a portion, as in 'dole out') both mean to allot in measured amounts. Paired, the near-synonyms make the verse itself sound like routine administration. 'Unequal laws' (l. 4) means laws that are uneven or unsuited to their subjects, or perhaps laws the people are not equal to; the phrase suggests Ulysses' impatience rather than tyranny. The line's heavy monosyllables and the enjambment across 'dole / Unequal' slow it down, enacting the boredom he complains of.

title: hoard, and sleep, and feed
short: An echo of Hamlet: a life spent only sleeping and feeding is the life of a beast.
body: The list of verbs recalls Hamlet's soliloquy after seeing Fortinbras's army: 'What is a man, / If his chief good and market of his time / Be but to sleep and feed? a beast, no more' (Hamlet IV.iv, Second Quarto passage). Hamlet goes on to say that God did not give us 'that capability and god-like reason / To fust in us unused', which anticipates Ulysses' refusal to 'rust unburnish'd' (l. 23). The 'savage race' are his own subjects, whose merely bodily life he contrasts with his hunger for knowledge; the line ends with the self-regarding 'know not me', a hint of the egotism critics have found in the speaker.

title: drink / Life to the lees
short: Lees are the dregs of wine; Ulysses will drink life to the bottom of the cup.
body: 'Lees' (OED) are the sediment that settles at the bottom of a cask or cup of wine. To drink 'to the lees' is to consume everything, even the last bitter part, and old age is precisely that last part. Shakespeare's Macbeth uses the same image despairingly after Duncan's murder: 'The wine of life is drawn, and the mere lees / Is left this vault to brag of' (Macbeth II.iii). Tennyson's speaker turns Macbeth's despair into appetite. The metaphor of drinking returns in 'drunk delight of battle' (l. 16), linking experience with intoxication.

title: the rainy Hyades
short: A star cluster in Taurus whose rising was thought to bring rain and storms.
body: The Hyades are a cluster of stars in the head of Taurus. Ancient writers linked their name with the Greek verb huein, 'to rain', because their rising and setting coincided with the rainy season (RPO note: they 'rise with the sun in spring at the rainy season'). Virgil twice gives them the epithet 'pluvias' (rainy) in the Aeneid (I.744, III.516), and Homer names them among the constellations on Achilles' shield (Iliad XVIII.486). 'Scudding drifts' are wind-driven sheets of rain and spray; 'vext' (vexed) means stirred up, agitated.

title: I am become a name
short: Ulysses is now famous, a name more than a man; Homer's Odysseus announces his fame in similar terms.
body: The phrase means both 'I have become famous' and 'I am now only a name', a reputation that has outlived the active self. Homer's Odysseus introduces himself to the Phaeacians as 'Odysseus, son of Laertes, known among men for all manner of wiles, and my fame reaches heaven' (Odyssey IX.19-20). The archaic perfect 'am become' (rather than 'have become') gives the line a biblical, ceremonial weight. The ambiguity matters: the speech that follows is an attempt to prove that he is still more than his legend.

title: cities of men / And manners
greek: πολλῶν δ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστεα καὶ νόον ἔγνω
short: A translation of the Odyssey's opening: Odysseus saw the cities of many men and learned their minds.
body: The proem of the Odyssey says of its hero that 'many were the men whose cities he saw and whose mind he learned' (Odyssey I.3). Horace rendered the line in the Ars Poetica as 'qui mores hominum multorum vidit et urbes' (he who saw the manners and cities of many men, l. 142), and Tennyson's 'manners' follows Horace's 'mores' (customs, ways of life). The catalogue that follows, 'climates, councils, governments', extends Homer's line into a Victorian survey of political and natural knowledge, and 'Myself not least' quietly places the speaker at the centre of what he has seen.

title: ringing plains of windy Troy
short: A Homeric epithet: Troy is 'windy' (enemoessa) in the Iliad; the plains 'ring' with battle.
body: 'Windy' translates the Homeric epithet enemoessa, used of Ilios several times in the Iliad (e.g. III.305). 'Ringing' suggests the clash of bronze on the Trojan plain, and 'drunk delight of battle with my peers' recalls the Iliad's picture of the Greek chieftains as equals at war. The line is the only place where Ulysses looks back to the Trojan War itself, and its Homeric colouring sets up the closing reference to 'the great Achilles, whom we knew' (l. 64).

title: I am a part of all that I have met
short: Experience has shaped him, and he has left a trace on everything he met; the line works both ways.
body: The sentence can mean that Ulysses has been formed by all his encounters, or that he has entered into and changed them, or both. A related Romantic idea appears in Byron's Childe Harold III.72: 'I live not in myself, but I become / Portion of that around me'. Tennyson's version is less mystical: identity is the sum of experience, which is why stopping feels like dying. The next lines (the 'arch') then turn this accumulated past into an opening onto the future.

title: experience is an arch
short: Experience is an archway through which the unknown world gleams; its edge recedes as he advances, like a horizon.
body: The image makes experience a frame or gateway: what one has lived through lets one glimpse what has not yet been lived, but the 'margin' of that untravelled world fades 'for ever and for ever' as one moves, as a horizon always recedes. The key word comes from Dante, whose Ulysses tells his crew not to deny themselves 'l'esperienza' of the unpeopled world behind the sun, and speaks of his ardour 'to become experienced of the world' (Inferno XXVI.98, 116-117). The image of experience as an arch is Tennyson's own; Dante supplies only the word and the appetite for it. The repetition 'For ever and for ever' turns infinite desire into rhythm.

title: To rust unburnish'd
short: Like armour or a sword left unpolished, an idle man rusts; Shakespeare's own Ulysses uses the same image.
body: 'Burnish' means to polish metal by rubbing. Unused armour rusts; used, it 'shines'. The image strikingly matches a speech by Ulysses in Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, urging Achilles back to action: perseverance 'keeps honour bright', while past deeds hang 'like a rusty mail / In monumental mockery' (III.iii). The same idea appears in the Hamlet passage echoed in l. 5 (reason must not 'fust in us unused'). The next sentence, 'As tho' to breathe were life', dismisses mere survival: life, for this speaker, is activity.

title: like a sinking star
short: Ambiguous syntax: the simile may describe knowledge (setting below the horizon) or Ulysses' own declining spirit.
body: Grammatically, 'like a sinking star' can attach to 'knowledge' (to follow knowledge as one follows a star sinking in the west) or to 'this gray spirit' (the old man is himself a sinking star, near his end but still moving). Both readings are active in the line, and they combine the poem's two directions: decline toward death and pursuit of the unknown. The westward star prepares for the closing resolve 'To sail beyond the sunset' (l. 60). Dante's Ulysses, sailing south-west, sees the stars of the other pole while 'ours' sink so low they no longer rise above the sea (Inferno XXVI.127-129). 'Beyond the utmost bound of human thought' echoes the Pillars of Hercules, the 'bounds' Dante's Ulysses passes.

title: Telemachus
short: Ulysses' son and heir; whether his praise of Telemachus is affectionate or condescending is a long-standing critical question.
body: In Homer Telemachus grows up during his father's absence and helps him kill the suitors. Here Ulysses hands him 'the sceptre and the isle'. The praise ('Most blameless', 'decent not to fail / In offices of tenderness') can be read as sincere recognition that a different, quieter virtue suits the kingdom, or as faintly patronising: Telemachus is 'centred in the sphere / Of common duties', a phrase that contrasts with the father's boundless striving. Critics who stress irony, such as Chiasson, see here the speaker's contempt for ordinary duty; others read a genuine, if distant, blessing. 'He works his work, I mine' may echo Christ's 'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (John 5:17), giving the division of labour a scriptural ring.

title: household gods
short: The gods of hearth and home, a Roman idea (Lares and Penates) given to a Greek hero.
body: 'Household gods' translates the Latin Lares and Penates, the protective spirits of the Roman home and its store-cupboard; Aeneas famously carries the Penates out of burning Troy (Aeneid II.717). Applying them to Ithaca is a Romanising touch consistent with the Latin name 'Ulysses'. 'Meet adoration' means fitting worship: the dutiful son will keep up the domestic piety his father leaves behind, which marks the contrast between the household world and the open sea.

title: My mariners
short: In Homer all Odysseus' crew die before he reaches home; Tennyson follows Dante, whose Ulysses sails with a small surviving company.
body: The address to 'My mariners' / 'Souls that have toil'd ... with me' is inconsistent with the Odyssey, where Odysseus' last companions drown after eating the cattle of the Sun and he alone reaches Ithaca (Odyssey XII.417-419). Tennyson takes the faithful, ageing crew from Dante: 'I and my companions were old and slow' when they reached the Pillars of Hercules (Inferno XXVI.106-107), and Ulysses rouses them with a short speech (the 'orazion picciola'). The final paragraph is thus a version of that speech. The change also opens a question: is Ulysses speaking to actual men on a shore, or to an imagined audience? Some critics note the poem never tells us.

title: men that strove with Gods
short: In the Iliad Greek heroes fought even against gods, as Diomedes wounded Aphrodite and Ares.
body: In Iliad V, Diomedes, with Athena's help, wounds Aphrodite and then Ares on the battlefield before Troy; Odysseus also endured the long enmity of Poseidon in the Odyssey. The line therefore reminds the mariners of a heroic age in which mortals could contend with divine powers. It also carries a note of hubris that Dante's version makes explicit, since his Ulysses is punished for exceeding the limits set for men.

title: smite / The sounding furrows
short: A Homeric formula: rowers 'smote the grey sea with their oars'; the furrows are the waves ploughed by the ship.
body: The Odyssey repeatedly describes the crew sitting in order at the benches and striking the grey sea with their oars (e.g. IX.103-104, XII.146-147). Tennyson keeps the formulaic order ('sitting well in order') and adds the agricultural metaphor of the sea's 'furrows', cut by the ship as a plough cuts earth; the plural also suggests the troughs between waves. Compare the slow, monosyllabic lines just before ('The long day wanes: the slow moon climbs'), where heavy stresses and pauses delay the action that this command finally sets going.

title: the baths / Of all the western stars
short: Homer imagined the stars setting by bathing in the river Ocean at the world's western edge.
body: Homer's cosmos is ringed by the river Ocean, into which the stars sink at their setting; the Great Bear alone 'has no part in the baths of Ocean' because it never sets (Iliad XVIII.489; Odyssey V.275). RPO's note glosses 'the baths' as the place where the stars seem to plunge into the ocean. To sail 'beyond the sunset' and these baths is therefore to go past the western boundary of the known world, where Greek myth also put the entrance to the underworld; 'until I die' makes clear that the voyage and the death are the same horizon.

anchor: the gulfs will wash us down
title: the gulfs will wash us down
short: The gulfs are the abyss at the world's edge; Dante's Ulysses and his crew are in fact drowned there.
body: RPO notes the Homeric idea that the Ocean river plunges into a vast western chasm leading toward Hades. In Dante's account the voyage ends exactly so: after five months, a mountain appears, a whirlwind strikes, and the sea closes over the ship 'as pleased Another' (Inferno XXVI.133-142). Tennyson's Ulysses names this possibility calmly, paired against the opposite hope in the next line. The double 'It may be' keeps both outcomes open and makes the courage of the speech depend on not knowing.

title: the Happy Isles
short: The Isles of the Blessed, in the far western Ocean, where favoured heroes live after death.
body: Hesiod describes the 'islands of the blessed' by deep-swirling Ocean at the ends of the earth, where some heroes of the Theban and Trojan wars live untouched by sorrow (Works and Days 167-173). Pindar places the virtuous dead on the Island of the Blessed and names Achilles among them, brought there by his mother Thetis (Olympian 2.68-80). RPO locates the isles beyond the Pillars of Hercules, in the Atlantic. The hope of reaching them thus doubles as a hope of a heroic afterlife.

title: the great Achilles, whom we knew
short: The greatest Greek warrior at Troy, killed before its fall; Odysseus meets his shade in the underworld in Odyssey XI.
body: Achilles died at Troy. In Odyssey XI Odysseus meets his ghost in the underworld, where Achilles famously says he would rather be a hired labourer on earth than king of all the dead (XI.488-491). Tennyson's Ulysses, by contrast, imagines meeting him in the Happy Isles, following the tradition (Pindar, Olympian 2) that Achilles was taken there. The quiet 'whom we knew' turns myth into personal memory and makes the comrades of Troy into the speaker's own dead, an echo, for many readers, of Tennyson's grief for Hallam.

title: To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield
short: The famous closing line: four infinitives in a regular iambic line, ending on resistance rather than arrival.
body: After a poem of hesitations and enjambments, the last line is metrically regular and end-stopped, a series of infinitives building to the negative 'not to yield'. 'Tho' much is taken, much abides' and 'that which we are, we are' prepare it with balanced, almost proverbial phrasing. The line has had a long public life: it was carved on the memorial cross to Scott's polar party on Observation Hill, Antarctica (1913), and has been used as a motto by schools and in public ceremonies. Readers divided over the speaker's character still often agree that this ending is the poem's most purely affirmative moment; ironic readers note that its resolution is directed toward death.
